See Bridging Condenser.

"C" Battery, a low voltage battery connected between the filament and the "grid" to give to the latter a negative potential. calibration, act of determining wave length, frequency, or dial adjustment. call bell, a device by which incoming signals, especially those of distress, attract the attention of the operator even if he is off duty. call letters, letters assigned by the Government as designations to all radio transmitters. capacity, the property by which a condenser stores up electrical energy; measured by the number of coulombs the condenser will hold when the difference of pressure between the two extreme plates is one volt. cascade, a series of condensers or stages of amplification. cathode, a terminal of an electric circuit. cat whisker, a fine wire used to make connection with crystal detector. charger, device that permits definite amount of electricity to flow in recharging storage battery. choke cells, cells which are wound so as to have great self-induction, usually over an iron core. choke coils, wire coils wound with iron centre. choking coil, a coil of wire wound in such a way as to have great self-induction. circuits, a circuit in which oscillations are possible and there is no distinct break of continuity is called a closed oscillating circuit; a condenser in which the plates are very remote converts a closed oscillating circuit into an open or radiating oscillating circuit. close-coupling, a term used when in a tuning coil or set of coils for transformer the primary and secondary are close together. closed oscillating circuit. See circuits. coherer, an imperfect contact or collec tion of such contacts, so arranged that when brought under the influence of the incoming electro-magnet wave it allows current from a local battery to pass and make some kind of signal. coil induction, a device similar to a transformer, which has a laminated iron core and a primary and secondary coil. compass, wireless, one of several forms of direction-finders, which enables an oper ator to get the bearings of a station transmitting a signal by turning a handle over a marked scale. commutator, a series of moving or movable contacts by which the direction of the current in a system can be changed. condenser unit, a system composed of two conducting surfaces placed close together and separated by an insulator. conductor, material which will freely carry electricity; wire, etc. continuous current, a current which invariably runs in the same direction.

Its opposite is the alternating current. continuous waves, waves with constant amplitude produced by multiplying transformers. converter, apparatus for changing potential of electric current. core, the iron centre of electro magnet. corrosion, action of elements in eating away metal parts of battery or outdoor antenna. coulomb, quantity of electricity flowing in one second through a circuit carrying current of one ampere. counterpoise, one or several wires stretched directly above the ground but insulated from it. coupling, the ratio of the mutual induction between two circuits compared with the self-inductance of each circuit.

Dictionary of Radio Words and Terms coupling, direct, where one circuit is linked to another in such a way that a portion of one circuit forms part of the other, or where there is direct electrical connection between the second circuit and a point in the first. crystal detector, the use of certain metallic crystals in a radio receiving circuit which have a property of rectifying incoming signal oscillations into direct current. current, secondary, current induced in a secondary coil of transformer or inductance. cut-out, apparatus having the function of a fuse, but not acting by the fusing of a conductor. cycle, period of alternation. cymometer, instrument for measuring the wave length and frequency of an electro-magnetic wave. cymoscope, instrument which shows the presence of minute currents; a detector; depends on its rectifying action on a train of oscillations. D damping, decrease in amplitude in a train of waves. decrement, percentage of decrease of amplitude in oscillation. decrement, logarithmic, a measure or the ratio of decay of an electric oscillation under the influence of damping. detector, an apparatus which changes the

Oscillations received through the antenna-ground circuit into audible currents. dial, disc mounted on shaft for adjusting rotating parts of set. dia-magnetic, non-magnetic. dielectric, a medium through which electric energy can be transmitted by an electrical strain in the medium. diode, vacuum tube which contains two elements, used only in place of crystal detector. . direct coupling, inductance coupling where primary and secondary coils are connected metallically. direct current, an electric current which flows continuously in one direction. discharger, the device in the primary oscillating circuit at which the spark or arc occurs. disc condenser, a variable condenser which has two sets of plates composed of semi-circular, interleafing metal vanes separated by insulating disks or air. disc discharger, a disk which has numerous metal studs on its periphery. These are capable of adjustment. The whole is rapidly revolved between two electrodes which may be either fixed or formed of rotating disks with or without studs. duo-lateral coils, a special form of inductance coils taking their name from their characteristic winding. duplex radio telegraphy, a system by which messages can be sent and received simultaneously without interference. dynamo, a machine which converts mechanical energy into electrical energy.

earth arrester, a small spark gap which consists of two brass disks separated by a disk of mica. The top plate is connected with the aerial and the lower with the earth. earth plate, a plate of metal which is buried in the earth, to which is attached the earth connection. earths, the metallic connections of the lower extremities of aerials with the upper crust of the earth. ebonite, a non-conductor based on vulcanized rubber. eddy currents, the stray currents in core of electro-magnet causing loss of energy due to induction pressures. einthoven, an exceedingly sensitive galvanometer for indicating received signals, in which the moving part is a fine stretched conducting string. electrodes, specially devised terminals which pass electric current through any desired substance. electrolysis, the disintegrating of a compound into its component elements by the passage of an electric current through it. electrolytic detector, a detector employing an electrolyte such as a 10 per cent sulphuric acid solution in a platinum container; platinum wire in contact with electrolyte is connected to battery as is the platinum container. Electrolysis due to current through electrolyte keeps platinum point covered with minute bubbles which act as insulators.

Oscillations from outside source of alternating current break through_bubbles, permit intermittent circuit to flow from battery through phones producing signal, electro-magnet, a magnet which is given energy by passing an electric current through its winding. electron, smallest known part of matter; principle of vacuum tube is based on theory of electrons. electron, the final unit of negative eleotricity. electroscope, apparatus for detecting small static charges. electro-static, an electrically charged body through which no current flows. 

E. M. F., electromotive force. Its unit is the volt which is the electric pressure forcing a current of one ampere through resistance of one ohm.

Dictionary of Radio ether, an assumed medium which is supposed to pervade all space and the interior of solid bodies.

fading, fluctuation of strength of radio signal caused by atmospheric disturbances. farad, the unit of electrical capacity. feed-back, the energy which returns from the plate circuit to the grid of the vacuum tube. The name is also applied to the means for returning it in the regenerative circuit. feeder, a main wire or set of wires. feeder negative, the wire which is connected to the negative pole of the generator. feeder neutral, the wire which is connected to the middle or neutral point in a three-wire system. The wire is common to both generators. feeder positive, the wire which is connected to the positive pole of the generator. filament, the heated element in the vacuum tube which gives forth the electrons. flux, a compound for soldering; facilitates the uniting of molten metals; magnetic flux, the flow of magnetic current about the field of a magnet. frequency, term used in connection with any form of rhythmical motion or change, denoting the number of complete movements or changes in a given time, usually a second. frequency, high, under the latest demarcation between high and low frequency, a frequency measured in thousands or millions of periods per second. frequency, low, a frequency measured in tens or hundreds of periods per second. fundamental, the fundamental note, swing, or oscillation of a system is the one which fits in with the formula giving the time-period in terms of those of its properties which affect that period. See time period.

galvanometer. See einthoven. gap micrometer, a short gap which is designed to protect apparatus from too high potentials. geissler tube, a vacuum tube which has its electrodes placed in bulbs in either end. generator, a machine which changes into electrical energy, mechanical energy. glass silencer, a glass tube which has wooden ends with holes to admit the discharge rods of an induction coil, thus enclosing the spark gap. grid, a frame of wire gauze or spiral between and insulated from the plate and filament of a vacuum tube. grid bias, a negative potential which is 

Words and Terms applied to the grid of the detector or the amplifier tube. grid leak, a resistance across grid condenser or between grid and filament for leakage of excess grid charges. ground, a counterpart on the earth of the aerial or antenna. ground wires, wires which give connection to the earth.

harmonics, waves whose frequencies bear & definite relation to that of the fundamental; the first harmonic of an aerial has a frequency three times as great as that of the fundamental; the second harmonic, five times as great, and so on. helix, a hollow core wound with one layer of wire. henry, the unit for measuring inductance; the change of amperage of one ampere per second, in an inductance producing a difference in potential of one volt. hertzian oscillator, a device consisting of two metal sheets or wings separated by a spark gap. They are used to produce oscillations which give rise to ether waves. hertzian waves, a name given to the electro-magnetic waves discovered by 

Professor Hertz in 1887. heterodyne, the production of "beats" in radio, brought about by placing one continuous wave energy against another and thus producing a beat note, which corresponds to the difference between the two continuous wave frequencies. high frequency, frequencies over a few thousands per second. honeycomb coil, a multiple layer coil wound diagonally in lattice like formation. hook-up, the diagram which shows the connections and construction of a radio receiver or transmitter. horizontal aerials, those which have the larger part of their length parallel with the surface of the earth. hot wire ammeter, an instrument for measuring amperage by means of the expansion of wire through heat. Indicated by a pointer and graduated scale. hydrometer, a floating instrument which measures the density of a liquid, for testing charge of batteries. hysteresis, the lagging of an effect behind the cause producing it; generally due to friction of some kind.

impedance, resistance offered by coil of wire to a current due to back E. M. F. impedance coil, a coil of wire which is wound around a soft iron core, inductance, the property of an electric circuit by which it tends to oppose any

Dictionary of Radio change in the value of the current flowing therein; the opposition being effected by the production of an electromotive force in such a direction as to lessen the change producing it. inductance coil, a coil of wire which is arranged so that it has a large amount of inductance. It is called also a choking coil. inductive coupling, the coupling of two oscillation circuits by placing coil of one in magnetic field of the other. insulating tape, a specially prepared tape for covering and insulating the ends of wires when making joints. insulator, a material which is a nonconductor of electricity. interference, the interaction of two waves of different frequencies, or of two waves of the same frequency, but different phase acting in the same circuit, resulting in the formation of nodes and loops. See loop. interrupter, a device for breaking up a continuous current into a succession of pulses more or less rapid. ion, an atom of matter which carries an electron, or an atom which has been deprived of electrons.

Words and Terms 

Oscillating current induced in the earthlead of the transmitter. The amount of glow produced by the lamp indicates the total current in the earth-lead, and the lamp is effective in tuning the primary and secondary circuits. lead, a wire which leads from one instrument to another. lead-in, the connecting wire and cable between the antenna and the radio equipment. leyden jar, a glass jar with inner and outer surfaces coated with tin foil. 

Used as a condenser. lightning arrester, device that will cause lightning striking antenna to pass to ground without harm. loading coil, an added coil used to increase the wave length range of a circuit. lodestone, iron ore having natural magnetic properties and also known as magnetite. loop, a point of maximum potential in a circuit or part of a circuit along which the potential is gradually rising or falling. When the aerial circuit is vibrating freely it will always have a node of potential at the earth and an anti-node or loop at its free end. ionization, another term for electrolysis. loop aerial, a frame, preferably four feet jack, a device into which is fitted the connecting plug. jamming, interference from undesired station. jigger, a form of potential transformer designed for high-frequency (oscillating) currents, and used both in transmitting and receiving. joule, unit of electrical work denoted by work done by one coulomb under one volt pressure. One coulomb per second equals one joule per second or one watt.

kathode, the point at which the current leaves the compound in electrolysis. kathode rays, electrons given off by the kathode of a vacuum tube. key, high-tension transmitting, a device by which the transmitting circuit is made and broken by a switch in the high-tension leads of the transformer, controlled by the ordinary manipulating key. kilocycle, the sum of one thousand cycles. kilowatt, one thousand watts. Also written K.W.

lamp, tuning, a small, low-voltage incandescent-filament lamp, arranged so that it can take a small fraction of the square wound with multiple turns of wire. It has directional qualities which have given it name of radio compass. loose coupler, same as variocoupler, which see. loud speaker, a device which reproduces signals loud enough to enable head phones to be dispensed with. low frequency current, a current having a frequency of but a few hundreds per second.

magnavox loud speaker, a device which by use of the electro-dynamic principal with a powerful magnet, increases the volume of tone. magnet, piece of steel wound with insulated copper wire, used in bells and buzzers. 

Marconi filings coherer, a glass tube which contains fine, metallic filings. It is used as a detector. mast, steel, a type of mast built up of hollow steel sections of semi-circular shape after a system which enables it to be erected to great heights without any scaffolding. megohm, one million ohms. meter ampere, an instrument which is used for measuring the flow of electrio current. meter volt, an instrument for measuring the pressure or voltage of an electrio circuit. meter watt, an instrument designed for

Dictionary of Radio Words and Terms measuring the wattage of an electric current. mica, a mineral insulator transparent in varying degrees. micro, one millionth. microfarad, unit of capacity measurement. micrometer spark-gap, a small, delicately adjustable spark-gap used to protect receivers, etc., against atmospheric discharges and other adverse influences. microphone, an instrument for magnifying sound. millihenry, one-thousandth part of the henry. millimeter, one thousandth part of a meter. modulator, a device by means of which the amplitude of one current in accordance with the variation in another current is varied. motor-generator, a combination of a motor and generator for changing one kind of current into another. multiple action, system by which one station can send two or more messages simultaneously to two or more other stations, and receive similarly from them. natural frequency, the wave length of any aerial or circuit without inductance or capacity devices. natural wave lengths, the natural length of waves produced by the capacity of the aerial and inductance. negative, the opposite of positive in an electric current. neutral wire, in a three-wire system, the middle wire common to both dynamos. neutrodyne, a radio frequency receiver which receives its name from the method used to neutralize a capacity between the grid and the plate in each vacuum tube. node. See loop. non-conductor, any material which does not conduct electricity. note tuning, the synchronization of the receiver to the frequency of the wavetrains, instead of to the frequency of the waves themselves. ohm, the resistance of a column of mercury 106.3 centimeters long by one square millimeter cross section at zero centigrade. ohms-law, the fundamental law of electricity by which it is found that the current in amperes which flows through a circuit equals the pressure in volts, divided by the resistance in ohms. 

Oscillations, eletcric, alternating currents of high frequency, such as are produced by the discharge of a condenser through a circuit whose resistance does not exceed a certain value in comparison with the inductance and capacity. oscillations, free and forced, an oscillation is free when it has the same frequency as that of the fundamental or one of the harmonics of the circuit, and forced when otherwise. oscillator, hertzian, a device for producing oscillations. oxidization, see corrosion.

period, the time required for the completion of a full cycle of an oscillating circuit. periodic time, the time of a completed period. photoradiogram (fō-to-ra'di-o-gråm), n. a photograph or picture transmitted by wireless. plain aerial, term applied to the receiving circuit when the detector is placed directly in series with the receiving aerial and the earth. plate, in the vacuum tube the positive member or electro. plug, a device employed to connect the head phones or loud speaker to the receiver. polyphase, a plurity of phases. polarization, the changing of the voltaic cell by depriving it of its proper pressure. positive pole, the pole from which the electric current starts on its way around the circuit. potential, the degree of pressure of an electrical charge. potentiometer, an instrument for varying and controlling potential in a circuit. primary, the winding of a transformer or coupler in which a current is impressed. radiating circuit, the circuit of the aerial radiation, the transmission of ether waves through space in every direction. radio (rā'di-ō), n. anything transmitted or received by electric waves; a radiotelephone; a radiotelegraph; wireless telephony; wireless telegraphy: adj. of pertaining to, or operated by, radiant energy; wireless. radio-, a combining form from the Latin radius, ray, indicating (1) connection with the radius of the forearm, or (2) pertaining to any radioactive property. radiocasting, the sending out of radio programs or messages from established stations. radiodyne receiver, a type of receiver which makes use of fixed inductances in transformers with variable condensers. radio frequencies, frequencies which correspond to vibrations which are not audible normally to the humar ear.

Dictionary of Radio Words and Terms radio telephony, the transmission of speech by means of electro magnetic waves. radiotron, another name for vacuum tubes, which see. receiving detector, an arrangement for changing the characteristics of incoming oscillations so as to make them audible. reactance, 'opposition to back E. M. F. to flow of current. rectifier, a device for converting alternating or oscillating currents into continuous currents, or into pulses of unidirectional current. reflex, the process of using for radiofrequency amplification and, following detection, for audio-frequency amplification the same vacuum tubes. refraction, the changing in the direction, or bending of electric waves. regenerative circuit, a circuit wherein part of the plate current is impressed upon the grid circuit through inductance -resulting in increase in grid current. rejector circuit. See wave trap. relay, an apparatus for opening and closing an outside circuit, through an electro magnet actuated by a received current. resistance, the property of a conductor which opposes the flow of an electric current. resonance, the production of vibrations in a body or a circuit by the action of a periodic force which has the same period as the natural period of the body or circuit. resonator, a box for producing sound. retardation, the retarding of the rate of the transmission of signals. rheostat, a device used to control or regulate the flow of current. rotor, revolving parts of radio apparatus.

secondary, the winding of a transformer or coupler which receives energy from the primary winding and delivers this to the secondary circuit. selectivity, the property of a receiving apparatus by which it can select or pick out the waves from the station which it wants to receive, to the exclusion of any other waves from other stations or from the atmosphere. series, an electrical connection where current passes through circuits successively. sharp tuning, the effect produced by a slight change in the strength of the signals. short circuit, two opposite poles of a circuit coming in contact without a controlling force. shunt, a system of connection where the circuit or instrument is connected in parallel with the main circuit. signals, the electrical energy which conveys intelligent or coherent messages. solenoid, an electro magnetic coil without the iron core. stand-by, notification to listeners to keep tuning positions for brief wait. static, atmospheric disturbance causing interference. static transformer, a transformer which has immovable parts. stator, a fixed coil in which rotor moves! as in variometers. step-down transformer, a transformer which steps down the amount of voltage and raises the amperage. step-up transformer, a transformer which steps up the voltage and lowers the amperage. storage battery, an accumulator of eleotrical energy. super-audible, a frequency which is above the range of audibility. superdyne, receiving set containing combination of regeneration and magnetic neutralization. super-heterodyne, in receiving, the process of playing off the incoming radio wave against a locally generative frequency. super-regenerative, the amplification of radio signals by frequently damping the circuit. synchrony, the adjustment of one circuit to another or of one transmitter to one receiver so that the time-periods are the same throughout the system.

tapper, a small vibrating hammer used for restoring certain forms of coherer to a condition of non-conductivity on the cessation of signals. taps, means of varying number of turns on an inductance coil; wire that is looped out in winding is called the tap. telefunken, a German term for radio. 

Tesla coil, fan oscillating transformer. three wire system, a system for distributing electrical current in which three wires instead of two are used. The middle wire is neutral and acts as a positive for one side and as a negative for the other side of the system. tickler coil, the coil in the plate circuit which causes regeneration by transferring energy to the grid circuit. time-period, in electrical oscillating circuits, time-periods are ascertained by the amount of inductance, capacity, and resistance in the circuit. train of waves, the group of oscillations sent out from an aerial at every discharge of the primary circuit. transformer, a device used for transmittance of energy from one circuit to

Dictionary of Radio Words and Terms another. This may be done either with or without change in the voltage. transmitter, a device for producing the sounds to be transmitted. tuner, the part of a circuit employed to alter the wave length or tune. tuning, the altering of the capacity or inductance value in a radio circuit. two phase current, a system of electrical distribution which makes use of two currents of different phase. It can be used with either three or four wires.

ultra audion, an audion which has a type of energy coupling so that a powerful relay action may be obtained. ultradyne receiver, a receiver which employs the modulation method, which is a development of the super-heterodyne. undamped waves, train of, one in which the amplitude of each successive wave is equal to that of the wave preceding and following it.

vacuum tube, a glass tube from which the air has been exhausted, containing a filament, a plate and a grid. A vacuum tube is used for detection, amplification, modulation and generation. valve amplifier, an audion type of vacuum tube which contains three electrodes. variocoupler, an instrument for varying the inductance in a circuit in which the primary and secondary coils are not connected metallically but by mutual inductance. variometer, an instrument for varying the inductance in a circuit in which two inductances are connected metallically in series. variable condenser, a condenser usually made of two sets of plates separated by air as a dielectric, allowing the easy and quick variation of capacity. vario-transformer, a coupling device to connect the tubes in a radio-frequency amplification. vernier, a device for adjusting any given control. volt, the unit of electrical pressure. voltage, the amount of electric motive force or pressure. voltmeter, an instrument for measuring 

E. M. F. or pressure in volts.

watt, the unit of electrical power used in practice. The Watt measurement being equal to the amperes multiplied by the voltage. wave-length, the distance between any point in a wave and the corresponding point in the wave immediately preceding and following it. wave meter, an instrument for measuring wave lengths. wave trap, a circuit which can be tuned to eliminate any undesired signal. wired wireless, the employment of elec tric power wires and telephone wires in radio transmitting and receiving.
